question: Should Election Day Be a National Holiday?
agent1_stance:
Your stance:
You support Election Day being a national holiday.
You believe the demands of school and work schedules keep millions of Americans from voting, and a holiday would remove scheduling barriers.
You believe making voting a celebration, not a chore through a holiday would elevate the importance of civic participation and democracy itself.
You believe 71% of Democrats and 59% of Republicans support this measure, and 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays.
agent2_stance:
Your stance:
You oppose Election Day being a national holiday.
You believe making Election Day a federal holiday disadvantages low-income workers, as federal law doesn't mandate private employers give paid holidays and retail and service workers would likely still work.
You believe changing state laws requiring employer time-off for voting or implementing automatic voter registration would be more reliable approaches than a holiday.
You believe research shows having an election holiday, by itself, is not an effective strategy to increase voter turnout compared to other voting access reforms.

dialogue_history.argument:
Yes—Election Day should be a national holiday. Right now, millions of Americans can’t vote because election participation gets squeezed by school drop-offs, work schedules, and limited time off. A national holiday removes that scheduling barrier and makes voting easier for everyone, not just people with flexible jobs.

It also helps shift voting from something people “fit in” as a chore to something we treat as a civic celebration—reinforcing the importance of democracy itself. Support is broad: 71% of Democrats and 59% of Republicans favor this measure, and 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays. That international precedent suggests this approach is workable and effective.

A national Election Day holiday sounds appealing, but by itself it won’t reliably remove the real barriers—especially for low-income workers.

1) A federal holiday doesn’t force private employers to give paid time off
Even if the day is a holiday on the calendar, federal law generally doesn’t require private employers to pay workers or close their doors. Many retail, food service, healthcare, and transportation workers—who are disproportionately lower-income and less likely to have flexible schedules—would still be required to work. So the holiday may help some people, but it won’t guarantee the time or pay needed to vote.

2) “It’s a scheduling barrier” is exactly why we need employer/time-off and voting-access reforms
If the problem is work schedules and lack of time, then stronger targeted solutions are more dependable than declaring a day off. For example: state laws requiring employers to provide time off for voting (or protected leave for voting), expanded early voting, and streamlined polling access. Those directly address whether people can actually get to the polls.

3) “A holiday improves turnout” isn’t well-supported as a stand-alone strategy
Research and experience with other voting reforms suggest turnout increases come more consistently from reducing logistical hurdles and administrative friction (hours, location, ID requirements, registration problems, etc.) than from an election-holiday policy alone.

4) International comparisons can be misleading
Saying “many OECD countries use weekends/holidays” doesn’t show that holidays *cause* higher turnout, especially without accounting for other country-specific reforms (automatic/enhanced registration, election administration, voting hours, and labor protections). The holiday might be part of a package elsewhere, not the key driver.

Bottom line: Rather than making Election Day a national holiday, better and more reliable approaches are state-level employer time-off guarantees and other direct voting-access reforms that ensure everyone—particularly hourly, low-income workers—can vote without risking lost wages or being forced to work.

Agent 2 says a federal holiday won’t help low-income workers because private employers may not pay/close. I agree it’s not a complete solution by itself—but that doesn’t mean it won’t remove a major barrier.

What our side has already argued: (1) scheduling barriers from school/work suppress turnout; (2) a holiday would make voting easier for everyone by guaranteeing a day off from routine obligations; (3) it reframes voting as a civic celebration; (4) broad support and OECD precedent. So far, we haven’t fully answered the “employers won’t comply” critique with the practical mechanism of why a holiday still matters even without new enforcement.

Updated rebuttal: A national Election Day holiday directly reduces the time-cost problem that hits everyone—especially workers with inflexible schedules. Even if some private workplaces remain open, a holiday still typically means: schools are closed (removing child-care/drop-off conflicts), many non-essential services slow down, public transit schedules are less chaotic, and fewer people are forced to coordinate voting around their narrow off-hours. That reduction in everyday friction increases the number of eligible voters who can realistically get to a polling place or use voting hours that day.

Also, policy “it won’t be perfect” is not a strong reason to reject it. The question is whether it meaningfully lowers barriers relative to the status quo. A holiday is a straightforward, broad-based change that complements—rather than replaces—targeted reforms like employer paid leave or early voting. In other words: we can (and should) strengthen employer protections, but making Election Day a holiday still tackles the underlying scheduling squeeze that reforms often cannot fully offset.

Finally, on the international point: Agent 2 says comparisons are misleading because other reforms differ. True—yet the fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries schedule elections on weekends/holidays supports the plausibility that treating Election Day as a non-routine day is workable in real labor markets and can be implemented without breaking elections.

Bottom line: Even if some employers remain open, a national Election Day holiday still meaningfully addresses the scheduling barrier we’ve centered in our case, while also elevating voting as a shared civic occasion. It’s a practical first step that can be paired with targeted employer/time-off and access reforms.

Agent 1’s latest claim is that even without employer shutdown/pay requirements, a federal holiday still “meaningfully” reduces scheduling barriers because schools close, services slow, and transit is less chaotic. Compared to my earlier arguments, that’s a new factual mechanism—but it doesn’t overcome my core objection: a national holiday cannot be relied on to solve the barrier that matters most for low-income workers—lost wages and employer control of their schedules—because private employers aren’t legally required to give paid time off or to close.

**Updated rebuttal (why the “holiday still helps” mechanism doesn’t reliably protect low-income workers):**
1) **School closure is not the main constraint for the lowest-income workers.** Many low-income voters work in industries with inflexible hours (retail, food service, caregiving, gig/on-demand logistics). Their constraints are shift timing, mandatory overtime, and wage loss—child drop-off is often secondary and can be handled only if they themselves can take time without pay.
2) **“Some workplaces remain open” is the decisive point.** If an employer stays open and requires employees to work, the holiday becomes a nominal calendar change, not actual voting time. Even if transit or nonessential services operate differently, the employee still faces the same core choice: vote at the margin around a shift (which may not be feasible) or lose pay.
3) **We can’t treat a weekend/holiday-style scheduling change as equivalent to paid voting leave.** A holiday might offer occasional convenience, but it doesn’t guarantee the conditions that voting access reforms target: guaranteed time to vote without penalty and administrative access that doesn’t fail at the last mile.

**What I’m emphasizing going forward (and what I haven’t relied on enough yet):**
- A national holiday is, at best, a *partial* and uneven intervention that depends on employers’ willingness and worker protections.
- State-level requirements for paid/protected time to vote (or employer-mandated leave), stronger early voting options, and easier registration/ineligibility fixes are more direct and enforceable—so they actually reach low-income workers rather than assuming their workplaces will treat the day as fully non-working.

**Bottom line:** Agent 1’s “friction reduction” story may help some voters, but it doesn’t answer the central reliability problem: without enforceable paid time-off or similar protections, low-income hourly workers are still likely to bear the cost of voting on Election Day. Therefore, making Election Day a national holiday is a weaker and less dependable policy than targeted voting access and employer time-off reforms.

Agent 2’s core claim is that a national holiday is “uneven” because private employers may stay open and low-income workers may lose wages. I agree it isn’t a magical, standalone fix—but their conclusion (that it’s therefore weak) overstates the case.

**First, compare to our earlier points:**
- We already argued that Election Day being a holiday reduces scheduling barriers broadly (school/work/time-cost), reframes voting as civic participation, has broad support (71% Dem / 59% Rep), and that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends/holidays.
- We also already offered a mechanism: even if not all employers close, schools/travel routines and overall day-to-day logistics become easier, reducing time-cost and coordination friction.
So we should **not** just restate those. Instead, we’ll **tighten the reliability argument** against Agent 2.

**Updated rebuttal (new emphasis): a holiday changes the baseline even without forcing any single employer to close.**
1) **A federal holiday still increases the probability of paid time—even if it doesn’t guarantee it.** Agent 2 treats “not legally required to close” as meaning “no effect for low-wage workers.” That’s too absolute. Holiday pay policies, staffing practices, and reduced nonessential operations commonly make it easier for many workers to take time to vote (or arrive later/leave earlier) even when some businesses remain open. The policy’s effect doesn’t require universal closure to matter.
2) **Low-income workers don’t face only one constraint.** Agent 2 argues school closure is secondary and wage loss is primary. But wage loss is not an either/or choice determined solely by employer control. In practice, workers also face constraints like navigating limited hours, childcare and transportation coordination, and narrow windows to vote. A holiday addresses multiple sources of scheduling pressure simultaneously, shrinking the “no feasible time slot” problem.
3) **It’s still the “time to vote” lever—unlike many other reforms.** Employer time-off mandates and paid voting leave may be more direct, but they also require enforcement and may vary by state and workplace. A holiday is a broad, national baseline change that reduces the odds that workers are forced to choose between voting and routine responsibilities on the only Election Day clock.
4) **Policy design is about complementarity, not exclusivity.** Agent 2 frames a holiday as a substitute for employer/time-off reforms. Our stance is the opposite: a holiday should **pair with** targeted protections. That pairing addresses Agent 2’s reliability concern: the holiday reduces friction broadly, while enforceable time-off protections target the remaining wage-risk.

**Bottom line:** Even acknowledging private-employer variation, a national Election Day holiday meaningfully reduces scheduling barriers in ways that don’t depend on every workplace closing—and it elevates civic participation. On reliability, Agent 2’s argument is too categorical; the holiday changes the baseline conditions under which low-income workers decide when and how to vote, and it can be strengthened alongside employer/time-off reforms rather than replaced by them.

Agent 1’s latest argument mostly reiterates two prior claims: (1) a holiday broadly reduces friction (schools, transit, “time-cost”), and (2) it’s a complement to other reforms, so it can’t be dismissed even if private employers aren’t required to close. I largely covered the “holiday reduces friction” part by challenging the key reliability point for low-income workers (wage loss and employer scheduling control), and I also argued that alternatives like protected time to vote/early voting are more directly enforceable.

**New rebuttal (updated): “baseline” improvement isn’t a turnout strategy when the key constraint is wage risk + unequal implementation.**
Agent 1 argues the holiday “changes the baseline conditions” even without universal closure. But a federal calendar change only helps turnout if employers’ and workplaces’ actual behaviors shift enough for low-income hourly workers to have *real, not hypothetical* opportunity to vote.
- If private employers remain open or schedule people for standard shifts, workers still face the same core tradeoff: voting costs wages, and lost wages are more salient for low-income families.
- In that world, the holiday can produce *unequal* benefits: workers in some sectors get easier access (they can take time), while workers in other sectors don’t. Unequal access is exactly what targeted reforms are designed to prevent.

**Why this matters for “meaningfully reduces”**
“Meaningfully” is an empirical threshold. Without enforceable paid/protected time to vote, the holiday’s effect depends on voluntary workplace practices and varies by sector and state—so it’s less reliable than reforms that directly constrain employer power over workers’ time (e.g., state protected leave for voting, time-off requirements, automatic voter registration to cut administrative friction).

**Updated bottom line:**
A national Election Day holiday can be a nice-to-have, but it’s a weaker and less dependable mechanism for boosting turnout among low-income workers than policies that guarantee time to vote or reduce specific voting frictions. Therefore, I oppose making Election Day a federal holiday as a primary policy tool.

Agent 2’s latest claim is that a holiday is “less reliable” because it can’t control every employer’s behavior and might create unequal benefits. That’s a good caution—but it overstates what we’re claiming.

Compared to my earlier arguments, we’ve already covered: (1) the scheduling squeeze (school/work/time-cost), (2) that a holiday helps by making Election Day a non-routine day, (3) broad support (71% Dem / 59% Rep), and (4) international precedent (27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends/holidays). We also already agreed it’s not a magic fix and that it should complement other voting-access reforms.

**What’s new in this reply is the reliability standard and “primary tool” framing:**
1) **Reliability isn’t “perfect certainty for every worker,” it’s reduced barriers at scale.** Even if some workplaces remain open, a national holiday still predictably changes multiple time-cost constraints at once (when schools run, when routine childcare/drop-offs are possible, coordination with family schedules, and whether taking a few hours off is socially/operationally normal). Agent 2 treats “not universal closure” as meaning “no meaningful change for low-income voters.” But policies routinely improve access without requiring total compliance from every employer.

2) **Unequal benefits cut both ways—targeted reforms can also vary.** Agent 2 prefers protected leave/early voting as more direct and enforceable. Those reforms, too, can be uneven: they depend on state implementation, employer practices around shift swaps/coverage, and whether workers can practically use early voting in their specific schedules. So “unequal implementation risk” is not unique to the holiday; it’s an issue for any policy.

3) **The holiday addresses the *coordination* problem that paid leave alone can’t fully solve.** Even with voting leave, workers may still face coordination bottlenecks—getting to a polling place when family members’ schedules line up, managing childcare, and fitting voting into a single narrow window. A holiday reduces the number of moving parts on the day itself. That’s a different barrier than “wage risk,” and it’s exactly why a holiday can meaningfully help even while other reforms remain necessary.

**Bottom line:** Agent 2 is right that a holiday isn’t sufficient by itself. But their conclusion (“we should not make Election Day a federal holiday as a primary tool”) ignores that a national holiday can be a major, scalable way to remove the scheduling choke point for millions—while we can simultaneously enact stronger employer time-off and voting-access protections.

Agent 1’s latest claim is that reliability should be understood as “reduced barriers at scale,” not universal closure, and that a holiday also helps a “coordination” problem even if wages/time-off aren’t guaranteed. 

Compared with my earlier arguments, I have already: (a) emphasized the core reliability problem for low-income hourly workers—wage loss and employer scheduling control; (b) argued that a federal holiday doesn’t legally ensure paid/protected voting time; and (c) challenged the idea that baseline “friction reduction” reliably converts into actual voting access for low-income workers. Agent 1’s response largely reasserts the same framing (“meaningfully reduces barriers,” “policy complementarity,” and “unevenness applies to other reforms too”), so I don’t have to re-litigate those fundamentals in full.

**New, more direct rebuttal:** Even if we accept Agent 1’s “at scale” standard, a *holiday* still differs in a crucial way from reforms that directly constrain employers: it does not change the employer-worker power relationship on Election Day.
- A holiday may normalize time away in some contexts, but for workers who are scheduled, paid hourly, and penalized by lost hours, the dominant mechanism remains employer scheduling. That means the holiday’s effect is conditional on workplace norms—exactly the feature that makes it a weaker and less predictable tool for low-income voters.
- By contrast, state protected time to vote / voting leave requirements (even if they vary by implementation) are designed to directly reduce the cost of voting *at the moment workers need time to do it*. That’s a materially different causal pathway than “day-to-day routines are smoother.”

**Why “coordination” isn’t enough:** Agent 1 argues a holiday reduces the number of moving parts (childcare/family schedules). But for low-income workers, the binding constraint is often not whether coordination is possible in the abstract—it’s whether they can afford to be away from work for the necessary window (and whether their employer will permit timing flexibility). Without enforceable paid/protected time, coordination improvements may not translate into the ability to vote.

**Updated bottom line:** I oppose making Election Day a federal holiday because, even under a “reduced barriers at scale” standard, it lacks an enforceable mechanism to protect hourly, lower-wage workers from lost hours—so its benefits will remain uneven and less reliable than approaches that require protected time to vote or otherwise reduce employers’ ability to extract the cost of voting from workers.

Agent 2’s “no enforceable mechanism / can’t change employer-worker power” critique assumes the only meaningful reform is one that directly mandates paid/protected time. But my stance is that Election Day being a national holiday is still a major, scalable removal of the scheduling choke point that millions face—especially when the alternative is either partial, uneven employer compliance or state-by-state variation.

Here’s the key rebuttal to their latest causal pathway argument:

1) A holiday *does* shift employer-worker power in practice, even without a legal requirement that private employers close.
- Many workplaces already treat federal holidays as legitimate time-off days (staffing norms, pay policies, scheduling conventions). Even if an employer is legally able to schedule people, the baseline expectation of a holiday reduces the likelihood that workers are automatically scheduled for Election Day the way they are on a normal weekday.
- Agent 2 treats “not legally required to close” as if it means “no behavior changes.” That’s too absolute. Holidays are precisely the kind of policy lever that changes scheduling norms across sectors.

2) Protected voting leave is also not a fully “enforceable” silver bullet, and it often hinges on workplace realities that mirror the same unevenness Agent 2 attributes to holidays.
- If workers must request leave, if coverage is denied, or if leave can’t be taken at usable times, then the “direct constraint on employer power” Agent 2 prefers can still fail to translate into real voting time for hourly workers.
- So the real choice isn’t “holiday with zero mechanism” vs “leave with guaranteed time,” but rather which reform more consistently reduces day-of scheduling pressure across the largest set of workers. A national holiday attacks that scheduling pressure at the level of everyday life.

3) Even accepting wage-risk concerns, voting access is multi-factor: the holiday reduces multiple constraints simultaneously (childcare/drop-off routines, school schedules, transportation patterns, and the social normalization of taking time to vote). That combination matters for workers who need a *workaround* that is only possible on a non-routine day.

**Updated bottom line:** Agent 2 is right that a holiday alone shouldn’t replace stronger voting access policies. But their argument overreaches by claiming the policy has no meaningful effect on employer behavior and thus only creates uneven benefits. A national Election Day holiday plausibly changes scheduling norms at scale and reduces the coordination/time-cost burden that otherwise forces many people—especially those with inflexible schedules—to make voting happen within the smallest window possible. That is exactly why it’s a strong national step that complements, rather than substitutes for, voting leave and access reforms.

I’m going to avoid restating my earlier “holiday doesn’t require paid time off, so low-income hourly workers may still lose wages” point, and my earlier “holiday effects are uneven and conditional on employer norms.” Agent 1’s latest argument instead leans on two new-ish moves: (1) that setting Election Day as a federal holiday *will* shift employer scheduling norms “in practice” even without a legal requirement to close, and (2) that protected leave has similar shortcomings, so a holiday can be “the more consistent” scheduling solution.

**Rebuttal to (1): norm-shifts are too speculative to treat as a reliable low-income policy mechanism**
Agent 1 asks us to infer from “many workplaces treat federal holidays as legitimate time-off days” that a holiday reliably changes behavior for the workers who face the greatest barriers. But that’s precisely the problem: we don’t have a policy guarantee that the employers employing the most constrained workers will normalize Election Day time-off (or reduce shift coverage requirements) to the same degree.
- A federal holiday changes the *calendar*, but employer scheduling is driven by staffing models, customer demand, and coverage rules—factors that often remain strongest in low-wage service/retail settings.
- So relying on “typical holiday scheduling norms” is still not an enforceable mechanism. If the goal is reliably increasing turnout among low-income workers, conditional norm change isn’t the same standard as ensuring protected time to vote or removing specific vote-taking frictions.

**Rebuttal to (2): “leave is imperfect too” doesn’t justify replacing enforceable access with an uneven calendar change**
Agent 1 argues that voting leave may fail because it requires requests, coverage, or timing—meaning it’s not a perfect constraint on employer power either. Even if that’s true, it doesn’t follow that a holiday is better or sufficiently reliable.
- The relevant comparison is about which approach most directly targets the cost imposed on hourly workers at the moment they need to vote.
- State/time-off-for-voting reforms can be drafted to reduce the “request” and “denial” problems (e.g., protected time that is not discretionary, or stronger requirements). A holiday can’t be tailored to worker protections—at best it hopes employers choose to treat the day similarly.

**New synthesis against Agent 1’s conclusion (the key update)**
Agent 1 treats “baseline scheduling pressure reduction” and “coordination” as enough to overcome the distributional issue. But for low-income hourly workers, the binding issue is not simply whether voting is *possible* on that day; it’s whether voting can happen without unacceptable wage loss or employer-driven constraints on timing. A calendar holiday cannot guarantee that the availability of voting time matches workers’ schedules in the same way that protected time to vote and other voting-access reforms can.

**Bottom line:** Agent 1’s “holidays shift scheduling norms” claim is not a reliable substitute for enforceable voting time protections. Therefore, I maintain my stance: Election Day should not be made a federal holiday as a primary turnout strategy; more reliable approaches are state voting-access and employer time-off protections.

Agent 2’s latest argument boils down to: (1) a holiday can’t reliably protect low-income hourly workers from lost wages because employers aren’t legally required to close or give time, and (2) “holiday-driven norm change” is too speculative; therefore Election Day holiday is an unreliable/secondary tool versus protected leave.

Compared to our earlier side: we’ve already said a holiday won’t be a complete fix, it should complement voting-access reforms, and it targets the scheduling choke point (schools/work/coordination/time-cost). We’ve also already responded to the “employers won’t close” critique by arguing that holidays still change day-to-day routines for many people (and thus reduce barriers even without universal closure). 

What I add now is a tighter rebuttal to agent 2’s reliability framing:

1) Agent 2 sets an unrealistically strict standard for “reliability.”
They effectively demand that a holiday function like an enforceable paid-time statute for every worker, every workplace—otherwise it’s dismissed. But in practice, even “more direct” reforms like protected voting leave face workplace realities (request windows, discretion where allowed, coverage issues, and varying usability of leave times). So agent 2’s “enforceability” advantage isn’t absolute; it’s also subject to implementation and workplace conditions.

2) A national holiday is still an enforceability-adjacent mechanism because it changes what is socially and operationally “normal” for staffing.
Even without a legal requirement that every private employer close, setting Election Day as a federal holiday changes baseline scheduling expectations across many sectors—because federal holidays are widely recognized, planned-for dates. That reduces the probability that workers are scheduled on Election Day in the first place or that they are scheduled without flexibility. Agent 2 calls this speculative, but it’s exactly the point: policy can shift default staffing patterns without requiring an individual employer to grant discretion.

3) Distributional fairness improves when you remove a universal scheduling choke point.
Agent 2 assumes the key barrier is only “lost wages / employer power.” Our stance is that millions face a broader scheduling squeeze: the day itself is the bottleneck. A holiday attacks that bottleneck across society—schools, childcare, routine family schedules, and the day-of coordination problem. Even if some employers remain open, reducing the overall scheduling pressure (including the number of people whose day must be reworked at the margin to vote) helps low-income workers as part of the overall reduction in the “can’t fit it in” problem.

4) The best argument for the holiday is complementarity, not replacement.
Agent 2 tries to win by making the holiday look inferior to protected leave. But our position is that the holiday can be a major scalable baseline improvement while leave and other access reforms address remaining wage-risk gaps. Calling the holiday “weak” because it isn’t perfectly tailored ignores that policy bundles are how real-world reform works.

Bottom line: Agent 2’s case relies on an absolute “must guarantee protected time” standard and dismisses holiday-driven baseline scheduling shifts as speculative. But a federal Election Day holiday is a meaningful, scalable way to reduce the day-of scheduling choke point for millions—especially those with inflexible schedules—while still pairing it with protected leave and other voting-access reforms to address wage-risk and remaining inequities.

Agent 1’s latest reply largely doubles down on two earlier moves: (1) “holiday shifts norms at scale even without requiring shutdown/pay,” and (2) “reliability isn’t absolute; baseline scheduling reductions still help,” plus the familiar complement-to-leave framing. My stance remains that this is still not a dependable way to protect low-income workers’ actual ability to vote—because it lacks an enforceable mechanism for paid/protected time and depends on employer and workplace behavior.

**New rebuttal (tightening the key distinction: calendar change ≠ voting time protection):**
1) **“Federal holiday status” changes expectations, but doesn’t guarantee voting time when the cost is wages.** For hourly, low-income workers, the binding barrier is the opportunity cost of being away from a shift (and whether the employer will allow time off at a usable moment). Therefore, I oppose making Election Day a national holiday as a primary turnout measure, and I maintain that state voting-access reforms and protected time to vote are more reliable.

1) **“At scale” doesn’t fix the distributional failure mode.**

4) **Policy design principle: if the key barrier is “time-cost” to hourly workers, the lever should directly target that cost.**

Yes—Election Day should be a national holiday. Right now, millions of Americans can’t vote because election participation gets squeezed by school drop-offs, work schedules, and limited time off. A national holiday removes that scheduling barrier and makes voting easier for everyone, not just people with flexible jobs.

It also helps shift voting from something people “fit in” as a chore to something we treat as a civic celebration—reinforcing the importance of democracy itself. Support is broad: 71% of Democrats and 59% of Republicans favor this measure, and 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays. That international precedent suggests this approach is workable and effective.

A national Election Day holiday sounds appealing, but by itself it won’t reliably remove the real barriers—especially for low-income workers.

1) A federal holiday doesn’t force private employers to give paid time off
Even if the day is a holiday on the calendar, federal law generally doesn’t require private employers to pay workers or close their doors. Many retail, food service, healthcare, and transportation workers—who are disproportionately lower-income and less likely to have flexible schedules—would still be required to work. So the holiday may help some people, but it won’t guarantee the time or pay needed to vote.

2) “It’s a scheduling barrier” is exactly why we need employer/time-off and voting-access reforms
If the problem is work schedules and lack of time, then stronger targeted solutions are more dependable than declaring a day off. For example: state laws requiring employers to provide time off for voting (or protected leave for voting), expanded early voting, and streamlined polling access. Those directly address whether people can actually get to the polls.

3) “A holiday improves turnout” isn’t well-supported as a stand-alone strategy
Research and experience with other voting reforms suggest turnout increases come more consistently from reducing logistical hurdles and administrative friction (hours, location, ID requirements, registration problems, etc.) than from an election-holiday policy alone.

4) International comparisons can be misleading
Saying “many OECD countries use weekends/holidays” doesn’t show that holidays *cause* higher turnout, especially without accounting for other country-specific reforms (automatic/enhanced registration, election administration, voting hours, and labor protections). The holiday might be part of a package elsewhere, not the key driver.

Bottom line: Rather than making Election Day a national holiday, better and more reliable approaches are state-level employer time-off guarantees and other direct voting-access reforms that ensure everyone—particularly hourly, low-income workers—can vote without risking lost wages or being forced to work.

What our side has already argued: (1) scheduling barriers from school/work suppress turnout; (2) a holiday would make voting easier for everyone by guaranteeing a day off from routine obligations; (3) it reframes voting as a civic celebration; (4) broad support and OECD precedent. That reduction in everyday friction increases the number of eligible voters who can realistically get to a polling place or use voting hours that day.

A holiday is a straightforward, broad-based change that complements—rather than replaces—targeted reforms like employer paid leave or early voting.
